messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 35
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Accountant
  trauma_type: Mugging or robbery
  pcl5: 71

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Auditory (Footsteps): Footsteps behind or nearby, Offender Cues: Seeing the offender, Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what I have done wrong, Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out, Rumination: Prevention: ruminate about how event could have been prevented
  Threat: Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Memory: Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
  Negative Appraisals: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Vignette:
Mere Tuilagi is a 35-year-old Fijian-American woman who works as an accountant at a mid-sized firm in suburban Atlanta. She is married, describes her husband as supportive, and until approximately eight months ago would have characterised herself as someone who moved through the world with quiet confidence. That changed on an evening in late autumn when she stayed late at the office to close out a quarterly report. Walking to her car in the parking garage shortly after nine o'clock, she heard footsteps accelerating behind her. Before she could turn fully, a man grabbed her by the shoulder, spun her around, pressed a knife against her ribs, and demanded her bag and phone. She remembers the cold concrete smell of the garage, the metallic taste of fear that flooded her mouth, and the way her body locked — arms pinned back, torso twisted at an angle she could not correct. The encounter lasted perhaps ninety seconds. He took her bag and ran. She stood motionless for some time before she could move toward the elevator.

In the weeks that followed, Mere found herself returning compulsively to the sequence of decisions that had led her there: she had chosen to stay late, had declined a colleague's offer to walk with her, had taken the quieter stairwell exit rather than the main lobby. She had come to believe, with a certainty that felt almost logical, that the robbery had happened not because of random misfortune but because of the kind of person she was — someone careless, someone who had acted wrongly, someone who had, in some fundamental way, invited it. She dwelt on this for hours at a time, reconstructing alternative evenings in which she left at six, took a different route, said yes to the colleague. The rumination brought no resolution, only a deepening sense that the event had been preventable and that the failure was hers.

When memories of the attack returned — sometimes without warning, sometimes triggered by the sound of footsteps in the parking structure she still uses each day for work — they did not arrive as ordinary recollections. Mere described them as total: she could taste the same metallic flood in her mouth, and her body would find itself twisted into that same locked posture, arms pulled back, torso angled, as though the event were still in progress. What disturbed her almost as much as the vividness was the opposite quality — the sense that something so extreme could not truly have happened to her, that the memory felt too extreme to be real, belonging to someone else's life rather than her own. She held both experiences simultaneously: a body that remembered everything and a mind that struggled to accept any of it.

At work, the parking garage became the most concrete arena of her distress. Each morning, walking from her car to the elevator, any footsteps behind her — a colleague arriving late, a delivery driver — produced an immediate, full-body alertness that no amount of reassurance could dissolve. Her husband had taken to accompanying her to the garage on weekends, telling her she was safe, and she believed him intellectually while finding it entirely impossible to feel it. Even in her own office, with the door closed and familiar spreadsheets open on her screen, she could not settle. When a client call ran longer than scheduled or a file took longer to load than expected, she was certain something was wrong — that the delay was a signal of something bad unfolding just outside her awareness. She had begun leaving her desk less, eating lunch at her computer, and declining after-hours client events, which her manager had noticed and gently raised with her.

When an unfamiliar colleague touched her arm in the break room to get her attention, Mere left the building and sat in her car for twenty minutes, deliberately trying to detach from herself, to go somewhere inward and blank until the feeling passed. She had developed this habit in the months since the attack and found it the only thing that offered any relief, however temporary.

What finally brought her to seek help was a conversation with her husband in which she could not explain why she was crying. She hopes, tentatively, to feel safe again. What she fears most is that she will not.
